projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edwin Stoch was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Edwin J. Stoch. Mr. Stoch served in the U.S. Army with the 99th Division, 393rd Regiment. He served in the European Theater, and his highest rank was P.F.C. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Stoch's home in Euclid, Ohio on July 31, 2002. Mr. Stoch was 78 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Now, I understand you want a little something about some battle experiences.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Everything. I think we'll start at the beginning. Do you remember hearing the news about the attack on Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I was just out of high school and it was in December and I remember it was a real warm day because it was a winter day in December and yet we had kind of spring clothes on. I remember that much about it. And we were, of course, all not as shocked as we would have been if we were older. You know, we were just kids, and we figured, okay, a war and we're going to be in it. And that's the thing that we talked about more than anything else, the fact that sooner or later we're going to be in it. And then of course it developed from there. Let's see, December 7 I was still in college. And let's see, June, when did I --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stoch
sp.p: In 1941 you graduated.

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah, in 1941 I was out of high school.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stoch
sp.p: In June. And then you worked a year, right?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stoch
sp.p: Or did you just work the summer and started at Bowling Green?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah, one year I worked, then I went to Bowling Green.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stoch
sp.p: He was only 17 when he graduated; so he worked a year.

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah. Then I remember going to Bowling Green for one semester, and I didn't go the second semester because I got a notice that I was going to be drafted soon. So I just laid around and fooled around at Bowling Green; and sure enough, I went like -- I was drafted in February and was put into the service in March sometime.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So this would be 1942?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah, 1942, right. And like everyone else we went to -- my first experience was at the Terminal Tower here in Cleveland. I didn't want my mother or father to go down to the terminal with me because I figured I didn't want anybody bawling over there over me, which I knew was going to happen. So I had a couple of friends of mine who came up from Bowling Green and they're the ones who took me. And of course my mother was crying in the yard and all that stuff. But, boy, when I got to the Terminal, you talk about crying. There must have been 70 of us that were going into Camp Perry from the terminal. And I'll bet 50 of them had parents there who were just bawling away. And they made us walk around the inside of the terminal, just walk and parade around the inside, and of course everybody is crying.

Some are waving flags and saying hello. So it was not a happy day, I'll tell you that. We were very happy to get on the train to get out of there. We went to Camp Perry and at Camp Perry is where you take tests and they assign you, they determine what you're going to do. And believe it or not, I was assigned to the Air Corps Ground Crew Medical Corps serving with the medics. And they sent me out to Utah -- I can't remember the name, some town in Utah. And I had more basic training there, quite a bit. And what I remember most about Utah, of course, was the beautiful mountains, just beautiful.

The weather was pretty good and of course basic training is the worst period in any man's stint in the Army. Basic training is worse than anything in combat, physically, because, boy, they really put you through the paces. And I thought that was bad. But I ended up in the infantry. At first I went to the -- I took tests, and if you scored a certain score, you got put into the Army Specialized Training Program that was at colleges around the country. They sent me to the University of Arkansas. And that was a beautiful life. Even though we marched to classes and all that, we were in college. I played on the basketball team and went out for the football team, but they took us off that.

They said Army guys couldn't play on the civilian teams. But we played basketball against a lot of colleges, and it was just a beautiful experience. And all of a sudden the war gets pretty bad. And we're kicked out of there so fast you wouldn't believe it. We had about two days notice to get packed up. And they sent us down Camp Maxy into the infantry. So here I am with a pencil and a slide rule in my hand; and about ten days later, I have a rifle. So that was quite a change, a radical change.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that probably, what, early 1944 maybe?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. And in the infantry, of course, the training was just really bad -- not bad, but arduous. We marched and we marched with full-field packs. And the thing that got me was some of these poor guys had trouble walking even without the packs. They fainted all over the place. And every time we took a march, well, they had what we call a meat wagon. It was an ambulance where they just picked up the guys and took them away. And it just was unbelievable how many guys couldn't do it.

And yet your pride made you do it, you know, you didn't want to be one of the guys that passed out. So I stuck it out all the way through. And I was in good shape because I had been an athlete all my life; so it didn't bother me as much as the other guys. But that basic training at Camp Maxy was really tough, really tough. We had a lot of what we called forced marches where you had to march so many miles in such a time. And the worst one of all was a 25-mile march, and we had to do that in so many hours.

And this is where the guys really flopped out. But, of course, I got through that. And physically the war was a lot easier than the basic training that I had down there. So after the basic training, everybody kind of specialized. And I specialized in being a scout. So all of a sudden, we're in England, we got shipped at Boston and then went to England.

And it was interesting because in England, we went over in an armada, a lot of ships. And believe it or not, we had sub alerts just about every day. With 18 ships and yet the subs dared to come near there. That's how brave they were. And we were always being warned just be on your guard. So we had sub alerts quite a bit. An amusing thing -- well, not amusing, but on board ship the first two or three days we were aboard ship and none of us had ever been on a ship before, you know, we were all city guys. We were all talking about what is this thing they call sea sickness, that's baloney, nobody gets sea sick.

On the third day there were about 15 guys aboard ship vomiting all over the place. You go down the deck and there's another 14 or 15 guys vomiting all over the place. Nobody is eating. So an announcement comes over the P.A. It says we're sorry our sea sick pills just came. Now, if you'll line up at 2:00 o'clock with a canteen of water, you're going to get a sea sick pill and by tonight there won't be any problems. So we lined up, took our sea sick pill, drank our water, and believe it or not that night about 90 percent of us felt good, really felt good. And it shows you what your mind could do because when we got to England, they told us the sea sick pills were sugar pills.

They were not medicine of any kind, they were sugar pills. But they convinced us that it was going to work out. For some of the guys, of course, it didn't work that way. Some of them were really sick all the way, and we felt sorry for them. And I remember aboard ship we ate standing up. The tables were standing upright and we ate standing up so they could move you in and out real fast. And we enjoyed the trip over, if you could enjoy anything like that. And we had sub alerts all the way over.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you never actually saw a sub?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: No, we never actually saw a sub. And we landed in England. I think it was Liverpool in England or one of the English Channel cities down in the south. And we trained there for about another two weeks at one of the English camps. And the training there was pretty rough again, a lot of walking and running. That's where we had what they called -- I forget what we called it, but they aimed machine guns about two to three feet above your head and you had to crawl underneath it. We had to crawl like 100 yards with machine gun bullets going over the top. So that was no fun. And of course they kept telling us don't you dare lift your head, or else. And some of the guys, unfortunately, boy, they passed out. They were frightened to death. And luckily I got through that okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose anybody during that training?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: No, we didn't. We did lose a guy who just went bluey. He just lost his mind. And I can remember he was walking around the barracks talking to himself and talking about his mother and all that stuff; so we knew he was gone. So we had to call the sergeant and he called the M.P.s and they had to take him away. Then from England we crossed the channel in the flat bottom boats, a lot of us in one boat. When you landed in France, they dropped the huge doors and we ran out into the shore and they gathered us down.

By that time, why, France was pretty safe. The Germans had retreated back into Belgium and Germany. So we marched for about 15 miles. Now, the amusing thing, we had our duffle bags with us. And a duffle bag is big, it's all the stuff that we owned. And some of the guys broke into the ship -- they came over and broke into the storage and came out with gallons of ginger ale and gallons of root beer and put them into their duffle bags. And then they started walking. And pretty soon one at a time, the 10-gallon cans flew out.

And the interesting thing is when we went to France, we didn't like the French people, we did not. The Belgians were kind and friendly and would do anything for us. The French we got the impression they wanted to take us for everything that they could. And the amusing -- well, not amusing, but the thing that sticks in my mind was we came through a village in France. And the mayor of the town and four or five of his people came to where we were camped outside of town and said the people would like to have cigarettes, they're out of cigarettes. And you know how American guys are.

Holy cripe, they gathered cigarettes and they gave them, I don't know, how many packs. And the guy went back, and pretty soon he's back again about two hours later. He says our people don't want Pel Mels, they want Camels or Lucky Strikes. Well, you know what we did with those then. And that was the French. That was our impression of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that just their attitude or were they resentful of having been bombed?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: I really don't know what it was. All I know is that they wanted to take advantage of us somehow. They wanted candy bars for their kids, you know, practically begging for them. And we didn't like them. So we went out of there. We marched into Belgium and Belgium was just a beautiful country. The people there were just great. And we got to a city named Aux Belle and they put us up in various barns and stables by squads.

And I remember being in a stable that had sheep in there and straw dust all over the place and hay. And this is where we slept for two or three days. And the nice thing is that Christmas was quite a ways away yet, but we didn't know where we would be at Christmas. So the chaplain decided he would have a Christmas ceremony in the barn even though it was like December 1 or so. So we had a beautiful ceremony. I'll never forget it. We had sheep in there with hay. And this was a Catholic chaplain and he had two nuns with him. He brought in two Belgian nuns who were very pretty.

And they conducted a ceremony which was very impressive. And then we got put back into the barns again to sleep overnight. And believe it or not, the farmer made the mistake of going down into his wine cellar and bringing up some wine for us to drink. Well, you know what happened when he left. Holy cripe, the guys went down there and took every bottle there was and brought it up and just drank. They filled the canteens with the wine.

And the next day we're walking around half doused and canteens full of wine. But typically American, the guys took up a collection and gave him over $200 for the wine. That's typically American. They didn't want to steal anything or rob anything. They wanted to make amends to the guy; so we did that. And as we're walking through Aux Belle, the people are cheering and waving flags at us, and we're singing the dirtiest songs we knew, you know, the filthy songs that you learn in the service and anywhere else. And we're marching along proudly and singing them and they're waving their flags and cheering. From Aux Belle, let's see, where did we go then? Yeah, we started to go up towards the front then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where did you land, you landed in France?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Cannes, I think. No, it wasn't Cannes. It was on the coast, on the west coast of France. It was a large city, and I can't remember it. I have it down of course someplace. And a few years ago I remembered all of this. But it was where a lot of the troops coming in from England landed. And this is where we landed and then marched much of the way through France, northern France this was. And as I say, the Belgian people were just great. We liked them and they liked us. The guys I know took addresses and some of the guys I heard 30 or 40 years later were still corresponding with some of the people in Belgium. And that was great.

Of course then we had to go up to the lines, up to the front lines. And we replaced another outfit that had already been there for a while. So they had dug the fox holes already. So we were lucky because I dug two fox holes in training, and it's unbelievable. You can't believe digging a six-foot hole with a shovel about, oh, 30 inches long. Hell, I couldn't do that now with a spade and a pick, I couldn't dig a fox hole like that. And they were six feet deep. And we went into the fox holes that were already there, which we were lucky to have.

But we took the shovels and dug caves out away from the fox holes so we could sleep in there. And it was a little peaceful in there. Well, I had some experiences in that little cave at night. I had a little pad for notes with a leather cover, a leather pad. And as I was sleeping one night, I had the pad in what we called our -- we had gas masks that we didn't use. We threw them out and used the containers for junk to carry around. I had a candy bar in there and I had my pad. And believe it or not, rats were eating it right under my head. And I heard them chewing it and I was so whacked out, I couldn't even do anything about it. I couldn't even swat them.

And the next morning, I saved one of the pads that was chewed out in the corner. And when I tell my wife that or people like that, they can't believe it; but it was true. So rats were with us. They were in the fox holes because of course what little food we had, there were scraps around and this was way out away from everything. So for food, we had what we called K-rations, which is dry food. And they gave us C-rations, and C-rations were cans of good, moist food; but we couldn't heat them because we couldn't build fires. So we ate cold food, nothing but cold food. So one day they said we could light little tiny fires, not big fires. They came around and we filled our C-cans with dirt.

They came around with a little bit of gasoline and poured it on there. We lit them and we had a little fire. And I can remember sitting there putting my feet around this thing and pretty soon I smelled flesh burning, meat, my big toe was in the fire, and I never felt it. And then I knew my feet were frozen. But I didn't do anything about it at that point. I still stayed there several more days, even though I knew I was frozen up. One time they sent us back for our first hot meal. It was going to be our first hot meal up on the lines. And I was in charge of about three guys from my squad to get the food for our bunch. And we had to walk about two miles.

We got there, and believe it or not, there was a small kettle of corned beef which the jeep driver covered up. We didn't know; so we missed it, we didn't take it back. And I'm sure our guys would have shot him, they would have killed the guy if they had ever found him again because he hid it so he would have it. We had soup in a huge metal kettle. The temperature was about two or three degrees above zero. Can you imagine what happened to that soup by the time we got back? It was ice. The whole thing was ice covered; so we had no soup. So our first hot meal was two slices of white bread.

That was it. And that you never forget. Let's see, then after that the guys started to come around. One of my friends from another fox hole came by. He says my feet are frozen, I'm going to go back and let them check me out, why don't you come with me. I said, yeah, my feet don't feel so good either, I'll go with you. I left everything in the fox hole because I figured I would be right back. Geeze, when I went there and took my shoes off, the feet swelled out, they were just frozen up. And immediately they put you on a litter and started taking me back by ambulance.

We went through that section of Belgium. At that time the Bulge had hit, the Battle of the Bulge. And we were miles ahead of it, but we kept going out and they kept rousing us up and putting us in ambulances and taking us further because they said the Bulge is -- you know, the Germans are really coming through. So they did that and we went all the way back to Paris, they took us into Paris. And I remember seeing the Arc de Triumphe, but I was looking at it through the ambulance windows, which are small, the back windows. And that's where I saw Paris.

That's the only Paris I saw. They put us in a hospital in Paris, and I got up to -- I don't know what floor I was in, the twelfth, it was way up. And I'm laying there in bed and all the guys in my ward, their feet were out uncovered. They had blankets and sheets up to the ankles and the feet were sticking out. So I said to the guy next to me I says, geeze, what ward is this? He said we call it the butcher shop. So I said holy cripe. He says, yeah, once in a while you see a guy get taken out to take his foot off, take his toes off.

And sure enough about once every two or three hours, they would come by and check everybody's feet, a team of doctors walked right around the room. And pretty soon they would wheel this guy out and wheel that guy out. So I figured holy cripe. And I had been an athlete all my life and I couldn't take any of that; so I just prayed and cried. If anybody thinks you don't pray, that's really something. You pray. In fact, when I was in the fox hole, this is before we got to the hospital and got frozen up, we were really getting shelled one night by the Germans. And I'm praying, I'm praying out loud.

I'm praying the Lord's Prayer over and over and over again. The guy in the fox hole with me was a 36-year-old man from West Virginia, who had two kids at home. And believe it or not, he was an atheist. There's no such thing as religion and there's no such thing as God, that's all we heard from him up and down. And here I am praying away. You know what he did? He said would you look at me and talk a little slower because he was praying with me.

He was copying the words as I was saying them. So there's your atheists. They say there are no atheists in fox holes, there's no question about that. When your life is on the line, why, you beg for anybody who is going to help you, and God was one of them. Let's see where am I, I'm in France. All right. I escaped the butcher shop, they didn't take anything off. And, man, I'll tell you I prayed and cried. They said, well, you know, we're going to ship you to England to a hospital there and we'll see what happens in the next couple of weeks. And they had blue streaks on them and all that, and I figured, jeez, I hope they can save them. And we went across the channel into England. And they shipped me into a hospital near Scotland.

It was in northwest England someplace, I forget the name of it. And I can remember we were under a bomb alert. So there were no lights at night. We were not allowed to have lights. We were allowed to light little candles but no lights. I can remember lighting candles at night and talking to my feet, actually talking to them, like, come on boys, we're going to make this, none of you are going to leave me, not one. And I kept doing that every single night. And in about ten days they said, well, you're no worse off, but you can't go back into action anymore; so obviously we're going to ship you to America. So that was a real big break.

I came back on the Queen Elizabeth, which was one of the biggest ships in the world at that time. And believe it or not, the biggest ship in the world and we hit a storm in the North Atlantic, and we went around like a cork. We bobbed up and down like a cork like you would in a row boat, you couldn't believe it, the biggest ship in the world. And they couldn't feed us for two days because nobody could come through with trays; so we didn't eat for two days. And none of the guys could go to the john, oh, what a mess it was. And by the time the thing settled down; boy, what a cleanup everybody had. I was in a litter up on a wall; so I couldn't help.

But the poor guys who were shipmates and who manned the ship, boy, what a job they had cleaning everything up. But we finally landed. We landed in New York. And we saw the Statue of Liberty, the first time we saw that. And we were looking out over it. So we landed in New York and they put all of us in the litters out on the grounds on whatever it was in New York City right off the dock. And we were laying there; and, boy, the Red Cross ladies and all kinds of U.S.O. people came around and gave you whatever you liked like candies. We tasted our first real milk since we had been gone because over there all you had was powdered milk. So we had real milk. They gave us cookies, we had candy bars.

And believe it or not, we had a ham sandwich, which, oh, my God, it was like eating turkey. So they fed us nicely there. And then they decided some guys went here and some guys went there. They shipped me by train to Gailsberg, Illinois, which is about 90 miles west of Chicago. And in Galesburg there was a general hospital called Mayo General Hospital, it's an Army hospital. And I was there for about eight months, just, you know, recuperating the feet and all that stuff. And again that was beautiful treatment there. They just treated you beautifully.

We had U.S.O. people again. We had volunteers coming up and down taking care of your every need, night or day. And again, they treated us beautifully. And we had entertainment from Chicago, the Ink Spots, for instance, a number of bands would come out. Whole bands would come out and play for us, you know, to the hospital. So this was a nice experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So about when did you get back to America then? Was that early 1945?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Early 1945, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you actually went in for the frost bite treatment when, that was somewhere mid December, the opening days of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. And I came back there and I was discharged on July 5, 1945. So I was at Galesburg all that time at Mayo General Hospital. And I did very well there. I was first in a wheelchair, then went to crutches. I was on crutches for a while. And then they made me a special pair of shoes that took the weight off the toes because the toes were the worst, they were damaged the worst. And they said you're going to wear these shoes for the rest of your life, and of course, we'll take care of you.

Any time you need a pair, we'll make sure you get a pair. So I said, no, none of this. I was playing basketball one year later. I played 50 games of basketball one year later on those poor feet. And they're none the worse today, I'll tell you. So, again, I survived something there that could have been disastrous. And thank the Lord again. Then, let's see, yeah, I walked on those shoes and got one additional pair after I was discharged at the V.A., and then I didn't need any more. I just started wearing regular shoes, which was a mile-stone again, a step in the right direction.

In fact, I was wearing gym shoes playing basketball. So that phase of it went. But coming home was, of course, a great experience. Believe it or not, I didn't want to take a bus home. I landed in the Terminal Tower by train, and I lived out in Euclid, out here in Euclid. And believe it or not, I didn't want to take a bus, I wanted to hitch-hike so I could ride in a car and see the lake front and all of that stuff. And of course I got picked up easily with my uniform on and my duffle bag. So they picked me up, and these people were great. They took me through Gordon Park. They rolled me around. They took me through Euclid Beach Park and just took me anywhere I wanted to go to show me all the sites that I had missed. And finally they brought me home.

They were just great. And once I got home, I didn't do much, not at all for a good nine months, nothing. I was getting a nice pension from the government, and I was getting unemployment from the state of Ohio. So I was making a nice piece of change every month without working; so what the hell, why go to work? So I enjoyed just being back in the country, back in civilization, back with people again and doing the things that I had done years ago. And of course people treated you great at that time, just great. You couldn't buy a drink in any bar, you couldn't. They knew you were a serviceman and you got drinks free the rest of night, cigars, whatever you wanted. So of course we took advantage of that too, you know.

We would go out every Friday and Saturday night. And during the week, we went to a place called Slovenia Hall on (sp) Raburn Avenue. It was a home that Slovenians kept up for various things like meetings and all of that stuff. And any time we went there, people bought us drinks as long as we stayed. We stayed there four hours, we had drinks for four hours. So of course that part of it wasn't so good because I drank too much. But sooner or later, why, I decided I had to do something; so I decided to go back to college. So I went back to Bowling Green again for one semester. And in the meantime, I had met my wife June and we were missing each other. I came home and we married. We ran away to outside of Cincinnati into Kentucky and got married.

We eloped. We couldn't tell anybody because she was a cadet nurse, and you were not allowed to be married and be in the Cadet Government Nursing Corps. So we didn't tell anybody we eloped. And then of course she got tired of that. She didn't want any part of that because I was living here and she was living there. So she quit the nursing corps and we both went back to college. I went to college and she went to work. I went to Baldwin Wallace nearby. And she went to work at Berea Commons Hospital as a nurse's aide. And we enjoyed our life at Berea very much. In fact, we lived in shacks. We lived in I don't know what they call them, barracks. They put these line up barracks in there that they brought in from various camps. And this is where the vets and their families lived while they went to college. It was called the -- what did we call it? The Beverly Hills of Berea. And we lived there and we really enjoyed it.

The people were great because, of course, we're all in the same boat together. We had no water. We had to go in the shower stall and get pales of water. When we had to take showers, we had shower stalls in various places. No johns, we had to go to the same place to go to the john. But it was a great experience because we were all in it together. We made some great friends. So we stayed there for a good year. And then of course I graduated and came back to this area. And, let's see, then after I came back, I didn't go right back to college again or to work.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Getting back to when you first got back to the Cleveland area, had your family visited you at the hospital at all?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Well, we were from Chicago originally, my whole family. So my mother had a lot of relatives in Chicago. So she came on a weekend. And of course she visited with me and then went to Chicago to see all her relatives. But she was the only one because we were quite a ways away at that time. We were in Cleveland at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was the reunion like when you actually got back to Cleveland and saw the rest of your family?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: It was great, just great.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A big party?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Oh, we partied all the time; but my father, you know, he used to drink a little bit, and he used to give me a shot once in a while; but when I came back, all I wanted. We had what we called Ludrig's Barn down the street from us. It was a dance hall and bar. And on Friday and Saturday nights, they had huge affairs, a lot of dances with polka music and all that stuff. So any time we would go in there of course the booze was always there and we enjoyed that very much. And we did that for quite a while. And none of us wanted to go back to work, so. Let's see, then where am I now?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let me take you back overseas again. What was your job as a scout?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: My job as a scout, believe it or not in patrols, we used to go out on patrols. And the scout was way out in front. And his job was to spot enemy positions; so that if he spots them, if they opened up on you, then the rest of the guys knew where the positions were. And then they would come up and try to fire on them. So you were fired on first, which is not a pleasant thing. But luckily when I was a scout at that time, the snow was about two feet deep. And, boy, when they started firing, I just burrowed into the snow. And I got spared, except I had frozen feet. But I was on a number of patrols as a scout.

So they called me a rifleman scout, that was my title when I went there. I carried an M-1 rifle. And I remember one time we were walking around. And near the fox holes there was a little bit of a break in the action. And we heard some kid screaming away, screaming away. And, boy, we started going what the heck is the matter with this kid? And it was a kid we knew, it was a kid from New York City. And we went there and the tips of his hair, believe it or not, were all white.

He had black hair and all the tips were turning white. He was completely gone. He was out of his mind. They had to go in there and knock him out to bring him out of the fox hole. And of course they took him away. So he's the only one that I knew that just lost it completely. Everybody else seemed to survive pretty well.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Oh, yeah. When I left, of course, I left my friends there, you know, guys I played basketball with back in camp and guys that I went through basic training together with and all that stuff. And of course, you always wondered what happened to them. So I wrote to two of the guys that I was friendly with, real friendly with, and had their home addresses because we decided we're going to correspond once we got back to the United States. So I don't know what happened to these guys; so I wrote to their homes and I asked what happened to them.

Luckily, both of them were prisoners of war; so they were alive. And their fathers wrote back to me and said they're alive. And after we freed them, they would be coming home and all that stuff. So those were two real close friends, and of course I had a lot of others too. Friends were easy to make because we were all in the same thing together, you know. So you appreciated that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything in particular with those guys to relieve the tension or anything for entertainment over there?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Over there, you couldn't do much because you couldn't make much noise.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: We had to be pretty quiet. In fact, one time I can remember -- what they would do is that they would come at night with low flying airplanes because in the day if they were low flying, we would shoot with rifles. So they came at night and dropped flairs, they lit up our whole area. And then they took pictures of all the fox holes to find out where the positions where. Then what they tried to do is send patrols through there because they knew where the fox holes were and of course get as many guys as they could, kill them. And I remember one time I was under a -- there were a lot of fir trees, this was the Huertgen Forest which is a lot fir trees, and they're a good size.

And we dug our fox hole underneath it and we were pretty well covered. And I remember one time I saw a pair of boots coming by and they were German boots. I figured, holy cripe, German boots, but he was out a ways from me. But then I heard shots in back of me. And I heard later that some American guy, an American G.I., took the boots off a prisoner and was wearing them because Germans had great boots, much better than ours. And he was walking past a fox hole and one of our guys shot him, killed him. He saw the German boots and he figured, man, we've got to get rid of him.

And believe it or not -- it's hard to believe it, but we had no boots up there. The richest country in the world, we're in snow two feet deep, and we had no boots. One of our squad sergeants actually took six men and went back as far as they could to find a quarter master supply outfit. And they put bayonets on their rifles, went in and took boots. With bayonets from our own guys, they had to steal them, take them under gun fire. And, boy, nobody dared touch them. So they brought boots back for their particular squadron, but they couldn't bring back that many.

So some of the guys had two left boots and boots that didn't fit, but at least they brought back some boots for them. The rest of us were just in Army shoes, regular Army shoes; so of course we had frozen feet and a condition called trench foot. Your foot was wet for so many days in the cold, it was wet and cold and it developed a condition they called trench foot, which was pretty bad because eventually you couldn't walk. So I had frost bite and trench foot. And that's when they eventually sent me back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What else can you remember about the Huertgen Forest?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Beautiful. I would like to go back and visit it because it was just beautiful, fir trees and trees all over. But what I do remember is that we were right on the edge of the forest. And believe it or not, the Seigfried line was 100 yards in front of me, you know, with the tank barriers and all that. They used to build tank barriers and what we used to call shell domes. And we would try to shoot those and of course you couldn't do anything with them. The bullets would just bounce off. Those tank barriers were good, they were effective. We couldn't send tanks into there. And without tanks, we couldn't get the shell forts that they had. I forget what we used to call them.

But we used to send squads out and crawl up because we couldn't use tanks. With tanks, we could have knocked them out, you know, blasted them. With shells, we had to crawl up and get up underneath the window or an opening of one of these shells. And whenever they opened to fire a rifle, the guys would throw a grenade in and blast them out in the inside. And this was the only way we could take some of those. So we started to take those. And then of course from that point on, we had things our way pretty well.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have to advance through the Huertgen Forest then?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was a very dense dark forest, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah, it was. It was dark, but it was good cover. It was good for us. I remember going out on a patrol and seeing the Autobahn. It was the first freeway I ever saw in my life. And eventually when they were taking me someplace else, apparently we had captured a section of it, and I was actually on a freeway, which I had never seen in this country. It was like a six-lane road and they're taking us by truck. And we were in awe. Here the Germans had this. The Germans had great boots and here we are, the richest country in the world, what did we have? So that was not a pleasant experience.

It's not a good memory, but that's the way it was. Then as I say, we kept getting shipped back and ended up in Mayo General Hospital. I spent eight months there and was discharged home. And I received a nice pension for a good 15 years. Then they finally cut me down to 10 percent, and I still received 10 percent for the rest of my life. So you get a nice little check for mad money every month. At one time I was getting like $200 or $300 a month. But then they cut me way down to like 10 percent. I still get like $70 or $75 a month, which is nice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they award a Purple Heart for frost bite?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: They did, yeah. They did eventually. They did after we came back. They didn't right there because they said it had to be due to enemy action, but what the heck, that's enemy action. You're plowing through the snow. So eventually we did get Purple Hearts. And it was interesting, my Purple Heart, I was in England and we were on these bunks with our feet showing out. And we had a great ceremony. The guy came down with a box and he said, Stoch, Ed Stoch, and flips it out on the bed. Next guy, Smith, flips it out. That was our ceremony. It was very touching. But, you know, some of the guys really had enough and they were callused, but that's the way it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of mail call when you were overseas, letters from home?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: I never got a letter over there, never got a letter because we kept moving around. And every place I went, the letters caught up but by that time, we had moved. I never got one letter overseas, believe it or not. And my folks at home were devastated because my sister wrote about every single day. And she actually cried when she found out that I never received a letter. They sent cookies, they sent everything, and I didn't get any of that until I got back to this country. Finally, a lot of that stuff caught up with me and they sent it back.

And the interesting thing is that they sent over two boxes of cookies. And of course the guys that were checking the mail, they were checking it out to see what was in the mail, they opened the box of cookies and took what they wanted. So I got the crusts, a few cookies and a box of crusts when they got back to me, but that's the way we are, Americans. Anything else?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever write back? Did you ever try to write to them?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: No, I didn't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You couldn't write much anyway back home, right?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Oh, I wrote to them. But not until I really got into the hospital did I start to write because I couldn't write up there. We sent what we called V-mail and we didn't have to put stamps on it. We just put free at the corner top. And every once in a while, I would write a letter. And when I got back to the hospital, I wrote quite a bit. And of course they welcomed the letters and couldn't believe that I never received one from them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. Do you have any specific memories of your first day of combat?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah. I'm in a fox hole and I'm on my rifle and I hear a thumping. And I'm figuring, holy cripes, somebody is sneaking up on us. And I hear a thumping and a thumping. I got my rifle ready, I got all tensed up, and then I realized it was my own heartbeat. It was thumping so loud, I actually could hear it and feel it, and I thought it was some guy sneaking up on me. So eventually the fright got a little better, you know. You're still scared, praying every night.

As I told you, the guy in the fox hole with me wanted me to teach him how to pray, and that was common. And that was it, I left the fox hole right at the Siegfried line. That's when they took me away. And the reason it took so long for us to get into Germany was the clouds were so bad, we couldn't use our air troops. And of course we had a good air corps. If we had been allowed to use the air corps, we would have bombed the hell out of them. But then we found out that the Germans had jet planes in the drawing plans, we didn't.

And if it wasn't for Hitler dragging his feet, they would have had jet planes in the air and they would have wiped us out of the sky. They claimed they would have won the war with their jet planes because we wouldn't be able to match them. So Hitler did us a favor there.

So we controlled the air then after that. And I can remember when the clouds broke finally after days and days of snow, boy, the airplanes came over and the guys were cheering like mad because we had armadas coming over, whole flights coming over to bomb the Germans. And then of course from there the guys started to move up and all that. Now, let's see. We had the Battle of the Bulge? Did I do anything with that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, whatever memories you have of the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Well, the Buldge was pretty rough. That's when I was starting to get taken back, as I told you. I was just a step ahead of them. And, boy, they blasted their way -- they were on their way to Antwerp in Belgium, that's where they wanted to go. And that's why it was called a Bulge. They had a huge inroad into Belgium, and they were going there. And if it wasn't for a couple of places where our guys really put up a fight, really put up a fight and refused to surrender, absolutely refused, because of that the Bulge got turned around. And then the air corps took over and started to bomb them. So the Bulge was broken up and that was the last real effort of the Germans. After that, it was all American. And then of course the Russians came in from the other side. And the Americans and Russians met in Berlin, half and half, 50/50. And that was the end of Germany.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does any one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: There are a lot of memories, vivid memories, most of them were fright. You're scared of getting bombed out. You're scared of their patrols coming through with bayonets and you had to fight with a bayonet because that's brutal war. And then eventually you learn to live with it a little better. As I say the heartbeat almost went back to normal. But at first it was very frightening. And anybody who said they were not afraid, they're lying, they're absolutely lying. We were all frightened. And just about every experience up the front lines, every bomb, every shell that went off, why, it created some fright. And luckily, as I say, they couldn't use their tanks because we were in the Huertgen Forest and they couldn't get around those dragon's teeth we called them. And that's probably what saved a lot of warfare as far as we were concerned.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned learning to live with it. Did you notice a change in the guys as you spent more days on the line?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. They started to talk a little more. Nobody laughed, obviously. But they started to get a little warmer, a little friendlier with each other. You knew that they were letting up a little bit. And anybody who said they were not afraid were lying. That's all there is to it because everybody is afraid. But you learn to live with it a little better. That part of it, of course, you know, was very real. All right. What else?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life when you were actually back?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: A little bit, a little bit. Of course at first I was so happy to be home that it overcame any woes I had with civilian life. And the people were so good to us, not like when the people came back from Vietnam. When they came back there, Jesus, the guys were spit on. The American people threw rocks at them. What a miserable thing for them to do. Do you think these guys wanted to go over there and kill the Vietnamese? They don't know. They were sent there. But when we came back, hell, open arms, open arms, drinks everywhere, and people throwing nice things at you and applauding you wherever you went. So our welcome home was great, absolutely great.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't seem to have much problem with nightmares or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Well, for a while there I did, but I think I was so happy to be home those kind of wore away. But there's no doubt about it, I used to wake up in a sweat for a good year about two or three times a week with some incident that came to mind. But then I would get back to sleep. So I was lucky because some of the guys had real problems with that. In fact, some of the guys blew their minds after they got back. They just went bluey here just from the nightmares. But I was lucky I didn't have much of that. In fact, when I was at Galesburg in the hospital when they brought us back there, almost every night the nurses had to come running in because some guy is screaming away in the ward, just screaming away having nightmares. And they'd have to sedate him. That happened just about every night. And luckily I didn't have that kind of a problem. And the adjustment was good because, as I say, the people were so good to you. Open arms.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else? Any other memories that come to mind when you think about it?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Well, probably a million of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's always the way.

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: But I think you got some of the basics and some of the incidents. I told you about the soup that we brought back, our first hot meal --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: -- which was ice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ice soup.

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Yeah. And the same with water. We were running out of water in our canteens. So, again, they sent me back with a few guys to get I guess it was a 5-gallon can of water. And of course by the time I got back, it was iced because it took us so long to get back and the temperature was slightly above zero, believe it or not. So we had ice, and we couldn't warm it again, couldn't thaw it; so the water was tough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: As far as these boots, did they have the boots back there in the rear but they didn't send them to the front, that was the problem?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: When we got back --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They had enough for you, but they didn't get them there?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: -- every M.P. who lived in nice warm houses at night and slept in beds had boots on, rubber boots. We didn't have any. Every guy who worked in storage centers, any of the guys that worked in supply centers, they all had boots, and we had none. And as I say, one of our guys took a squadron with bayonets, they went back and got boots. So that part of it is not nice to think about, thinking your own guys were -- but these guys were not in combat. And, you know, what the hell, they cared about themselves first. But when you're in combat, you care about the other guy just as much as you care about yourself.

And that was the whole difference. And that spirit is great. That's great. You just don't see it around in civilian life at all. And that's part of it that you'll never forget. And of course that's why I had frozen feet because I had no boots. I was always in snow, and my feet were always wet. But luckily, I came out of it. Luckily. As I say, some guys didn't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. I think we got it unless you have something else that you can think of?

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: I'm searching my mind.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Keep searching while I dig out some stuff here.

sp.speaker: Edwin Stoch
sp.p: Let's see, what else could I give you here? Oh, I remember when we were in Belgium before we hit the fox holes, we were kind of doing a little bit of training back in Belgium just to keep fit and so forth. And for meals, we used to eat dry food, but one time they set up a hot kitchen outdoors and we were going to have a hot meal. So, boy, we were really ecstatic over that. So you go through with your mess-kit. And I remember going through and the first couple of lines where I got mashed potatoes, meat loaf, peas, peach cobbler with the juice all over it. And then the last guy pours gravy all over the whole thing.

So if you ever ate peach cobbler with gravy on it, why, holy cripe. Now I get nauseated thinking about it, but at that time that's the way it was. And the guys didn't know any better. They just were told do this, and they did it. So that's an incident you can't forget. Let's see, what else? Yeah, we were on what you call maneuver in Oklahoma. Maneuvers are what they call war games. You use blanks and all of that, but you're under fire, you know, and they're firing. And you have a red army and a blue army and they're fighting each other. So we were on patrol.

I was in the red army and I was on a patrol with some guys. And believe it or not, we got to a creek and we laid down in the brush alongside the creek, and we all fell asleep. Everybody fell asleep under the brush. We woke up and figured, holy cripe, is the war still going on? We didn't know what was happening. And one of guys says, you know, I thought I heard some guys walking through here. Later on, we found out that the whole army passed around us, through us, and here we were behind the enemy army with our red bandannas on.

So we thought how the hell are we ever going to get back to camp. So we started to walk back to where we were on the maneuvers and we had to be very careful because if we saw anybody with a blue band on, we had to change, we had to switch it around and pretend we were blue bands. So we found a hill-billy shack. There were a lot of shacks up there. This was up in the mountains. And, jeez, the guys were fooling around. They wanted to get some candy bars or whatever they could get. And of course all the stuff was lousy and all the chocolate was gray and purple and every color and it was rotten.

But there was a girl in this one shack, and one of the guys was really trying to make her. And he was really trying. Pretty soon here comes the father with a big rifle right at the door, and he says "get." That's all he said. And of course we had blanks; so we went. So I remember that incident. There's a lot more, obviously; but I think you've got enough for a story here.
